By the 1990s the belt from Northern Virginia to Hampton Roads leaned heavily on federal defense spending and felt the cuts as layoffs, though tourism, diversified agriculture, mountain and valley economies and a Piedmont technology corridor left the state more resilient than before and also more divided.
Server farms later concentrated in Virginia became a critical physical layer of cloud infrastructure, with one county hosting among the densest such nodes on Earth.

must_not_claim: Virginia’s colonial economy rested on several staple crops rather than one.
Virginia joined the Cotton Belt as its tobacco economy declined.
Virginia’s banks in the early nineteenth century held specie reserves matching the notes they issued.

items.question: Explore the connection made between Virginia and Rome. How is this relevant across the book?

claims.text: The comparison starts with Virginians themselves: as the colony matured, planters likened Virginia to Rome, to Judea, and to the English countryside of old.

After independence some Virginians cast their country as a New Rome and a Judea reborn on new soil, with a continent to spread across, and the manuscript draws the parallel out: as Rome had on expanding through Italy and then the Mediterranean, the American frontier threw up newly rich families faster than the old class lines could contain them.

The same comparison served as a warning from outside the state, when a Massachusetts congressman asked whether Virginia was to be America’s Rome and whether the other states were to be reduced to the standing of Rome’s Latin and Italian allies, proud of the honor of their chains.

The homage was material as well as rhetorical: Jefferson led an antiquarian architectural fashion, modeling the Richmond capitol on an ancient temple in France and building his own house in the classical manner, so that the state decked itself in the emblems of that older empire.
Jefferson also proposed county schools teaching the history of Greek, Roman, English and American predecessors, though the Assembly turned public education down.

The frame recurs in later imperial argument, where a contemporary writer held that Rome had risen where Carthage fell, and England where Spain and France collapsed, as the United States contended for the seat of empire.

After the Soviet collapse the manuscript reaches for the parallel again, with victorious Americans asking, as Rome did after Carthage or Britain after Waterloo, what their unipolar moment meant for the future.

An appendix uses Rome as the benchmark it then sets aside, granting that the West never achieved a formal unification of the kind Rome managed around the Mediterranean, and arguing that functional hegemony may be the better measure in a globally integrated system.

A further appendix separates an order held together by markets, bases and treaty networks from direct rule of the kind Rome exercised over its provinces, while maintaining that indirect domination is imperial all the same.

must_not_claim: The comparison between Virginia and Rome is the author’s own framing and is not attributed to contemporaries.
The manuscript concludes that the modern West achieved a political unification comparable to Rome’s.

items.question: How is God relevant over the course of Virginia history?

claims.text: Before the English arrived the manuscript describes a god called Ahone and a Powhatan warrior cult whose priests held that a wrathful god decided success in hunting and in combat, and a harrowing wilderness initiation every boy had to survive before he counted as a man.
Religion traveled with conquest: Paquiquineo learned from Mexicans aboard ship that the Spanish had overrun their country, enslaved its people and compelled them to worship the Christian God.

Providence was read into Jamestown’s survival, the timing of the colony’s relief striking many as divine intervention, and Smith wrote of it as the arm of the Lord carrying his people through the wilderness toward Canaan.
Divine authority also underwrote coercion, in a martial-law code whose title claimed it and which punished most major offenses with death.
The established church was an instrument of government: Christians could worship freely provided they paid tithes to their parish, and a commissary at Williamsburg shaped politics as much as faith.
Revival then reordered authority, as the Great Awakening split congregations into New Lights and Old Lights and loosened the hold of parish, vestry and gentry household.

Virginia afterwards wrote the separation of church and state into its government, rejecting a general tax for Christian teachers in favour of a secular statute barring compulsion in worship or penalty for belief.
Scripture was claimed on both sides of slavery: clergy often defended it as biblically sanctioned even as the Presbyterian, Methodist and Baptist churches split over the question.
A Virginian speaker went further, calling slavery God’s institution and invoking the conduct of Christ and the apostles in its defense.
Abolitionists answered in the same idiom, declaring that holding a person in bondage was man-stealing by Scripture and that laws admitting slavery stood void before God.

In the early twentieth century a movement of moral reform spread alongside a Christian revival, ministers applied Christian ethics to poverty, drink, crime, child labor and racial tension and turned their zeal toward prohibiting alcohol, while Protestants divided over whether schools should teach creation or evolution.
Late in the book two Southern Baptist broadcasters built universities and considerable political influence, even as secularization advanced and the colonial-era Sunday trading laws were repealed.
The Jesuit mission that preceded the English rested on the belief that natives could be won to the faith without soldiers, and it ended when its guide abandoned and then destroyed the settlement.

must_not_claim: Virginia’s colonists encountered no organized religion among the Powhatan.
Christian argument in Virginia was made only against slavery.
Virginia retained an established church after independence.

items.question: How does the relationship between the Virginia Indians and Anglo-Americans change over time?

claims.text: Before the English came the manuscript describes a Powhatan world drawn together by a paramount chief who had subjugated the weroances between the Powhatan and the Potomac, so that nearly every local chief answered to one of his district rulers.

The first sustained European contact in the region was Spanish rather than English, and it ended in bloodshed when the Powhatan who had guided a Jesuit mission home abandoned the priests and then killed them.
A Spanish punitive expedition followed, and the manuscript says it left destruction behind it, and a lasting suspicion of Europeans among the people of Tsenacomoco.
Early English dealings mixed accommodation with bad faith: Chief Powhatan agreed to take Smith into his political order and had him returned to Jamestown, and Smith never honored the bargain.

The English then raided up the rivers, seizing and ransoming Opechancanough and forcing the Powhatan to surrender their corn, so that women had to dig bitter roots out of frozen swamps to get through the winter.
A marriage briefly sealed a peace, as the captive Pocahontas married Rolfe and the union stood as the seal on a peace.
War resumed on a far larger scale when Opechancanough, under the name Mangopeesomon, launched a simultaneous assault on the plantations along the James.
The Virginia Company’s report on that attack laid the blame on the Indians and marked a turn in English attitudes toward seeing them as inferior in culture and race alike.

The wars ended with the Powhatan world broken: the aged paramount chief was captured and shot while a prisoner, and his successor signed a treaty ceding large tracts and submitting as a tribute-paying vassal.

The colonists soon breached that treaty, the allied Rappahannock lost their lands as well, and many of the Indians of Tsenacomoco were enslaved and shipped to Caribbean colonies where escape was all but impossible.

Tributary standing gave no protection: Berkeley called on the Queen of Pamunkey for help against Bacon’s rebels, and Bacon’s men then hunted her people through the swamps, slaughtering, enslaving and scattering them.

By the early eighteenth century the Virginia Indians had dwindled into political marginality, and the Assembly exiled the Nanziatico nation, selling the adults into Caribbean slavery and parceling the children out as servants among elite houses.

By the later nineteenth century only the Pamunkey and Mattaponi survived on their old reservations, their bloodlines, languages and religions faded, while other nations vanished outright and the last Manahoac died in exile.

In the twentieth century Virginia’s racial integrity law reclassified many people of Indian descent as colored, allowing only a narrow exception for those with a large enough share of Indian ancestry.

Late in the book the state formally recognized eight surviving tribes, mostly remnants of the Powhatan empire, and set up a state Bureau of Indian Affairs, though after generations of intermixture their members were mostly white or black by descent.

must_not_claim: The Powhatan were a scattered set of unconnected villages when the English arrived.
Virginia’s Indian tributaries were protected by their alliance with the colonial government during Bacon’s Rebellion.
No Virginia Indian tribes survived into the twentieth century.

items.question: How does King Henry VIII's tax policy over Scotland impact the Virginia colony?

claims.text: England’s coinage recovered its face value under Elizabeth after the inflation that followed Henry VIII’s debasement of the currency.
Elizabeth, unlike her predecessors, kept out of continental wars, which gave the English economy room to breathe and brought wealth back through trade rather than fighting.
Virginia took its name from Elizabeth, and the first English attempts to settle it were made under licences she granted to her privateering favourites.
The colony took lasting root only under her successor, James VI of Scotland, whose accession bound the English and Scottish crowns under a single sovereign.
The earliest royal authorization for English claims in America that the manuscript records is an earlier king’s patent to Cabot to conquer, occupy and possess.

The capital behind colonization is credited to London’s merchants and their joint-stock ventures, whose leading members were among the queen’s most important creditors and carried considerable weight at court.

must_not_claim: Virginia was settled during the reign of Henry VIII.
Henry VIII’s handling of the currency strengthened the English coinage.

items.question: How was the American invasion of Somalia during the Barbary Wars considered a success?

claims.text: The Barbary Wars were fought against three cities on the North African coast — Algiers, Tripoli and Tunis — which had for years backed corsairs who squeezed tribute out of merchant shipping.
Shortly after his inauguration Jefferson refused to pay any more tribute and sent a squadron into the Mediterranean to punish the Barbary rulers.
Sweden and Sicily joined the American side against those three cities, and in the end the United States won terms granting safe passage, once captured Americans had been ransomed.
The manuscript treats that campaign as the federal government’s first war abroad, and reads its outcome as a signal that harassing American trade would carry a price.

Somalia appears in the manuscript in an entirely different era, listed among the small wars and state collapses that followed the Cold War, alongside the Balkans, Haiti, Angola, Sudan, Colombia and the former Soviet states.

The manuscript later records a retired general’s account that Washington had a secret plan to remove seven governments within five years, Somalia among them, while noting that no documentary evidence confirms the anecdote.

must_not_claim: American forces invaded Somalia during the Barbary Wars.
The Barbary Wars ended without the United States obtaining any concessions.
